readerTitle: Your new shift lead says it was fine. You say it wasn't.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페 저녁 교대 리더, 물류창고 야간 리더) · 적용 레슨이며 수치나 연구 인용 없음
insight: 새 리더의 실수처럼 보이는 문제는 대개 '완료'의 기준을 서로 다르게 알고 있어서 생기며, 기대치를 먼저 맞춰야 피드백도 효과가 있다.
misconception: 일을 잘하던 직원이면 리더로 올려도 알아서 잘할 것이고, 문제가 생기면 지적만 하면 고쳐진다.

sources.text: PPL-02-05 Setting expectations, PPL-02-03 Giving feedback 레슨의 개념을 적용

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상이며 통계나 연구 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 기대치의 네 요소(결과, 기준, 기한, 확인 방법)와 피드백 방식(빠르게, 구체적 행동, 영향, 질문)이 PPL-02-05, PPL-02-03 레슨의 용어·구성과 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
8번 카드의 창고 장면(팔레트 스캔 확인)은 일반적인 출고 검수 방식을 단순화한 설명입니다. 특정 업계 기준으로 제시하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your new shift lead says it was fine. You say it wasn't.
body: You promoted Sam, your best barista, to evening shift lead. Three weeks in, the morning crew keeps arriving to the same mess: no cups restocked, the fridge log blank, the grinder half cleaned.
You ask Sam about it. He looks surprised. "We closed. Everything was clean and locked."

image.label: Café counter at opening time with an empty cup stack and a blank log sheet
image.brief: 이른 아침 카페 카운터. 빈 컵 거치대, 비어 있는 냉장고 온도 기록지, 반쯤 닦인 그라인더. 오픈 직원이 팔짱을 끼고 서 있음. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤, 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: Sam is reliable and well liked. You want him to succeed as a lead, and you want calm mornings.

options.text: Text Sam a list of everything the morning crew found
options.feedback: It's honest and fast, but it's feedback on a standard Sam never agreed to. He'll fix these items and miss the next ones.

options.text: Sit down with Sam and agree what a finished close looks like and how you'll both check it
options.feedback: This is **setting expectations**. It costs half an hour now and fixes the cause, not just this week's symptoms.

options.text: Work the next few closes alongside Sam to show him how
options.feedback: Showing helps, but you're doing his job again. Without a shared definition of done, the gap returns when you leave.

cards.title: "Closed" meant two different things.
body: To Sam, closing meant clean surfaces and a locked door. That's what it meant when he was a barista, and he did it well.
To you, closing meant the café was ready for the opener: cups stocked, fridge temperatures logged, grinder stripped down. You never said so. You just knew it.
Sam wasn't careless. He was hitting a target only you could see.

cards.title: Make "done" visible.
body: You and Sam write the close down together. The **outcome** comes first, so Sam can judge anything the checklist misses.

breakdown.label: What success looks like
breakdown.detail: The opener can serve the first customer within 10 minutes

breakdown.label: The must-dos
breakdown.detail: Cups stocked, fridge log filled, grinder cleaned

breakdown.label: How you'll both know
breakdown.detail: Opener sends a thumbs up or a photo of what's missing

cards.softwareNote: A new on-call lead hits the same gap. "Handle incidents" can mean reply within 15 minutes or find the root cause. Write down the outcome, the standard and the check before the first bad night.

cards.title: The closes are fixed. Now there's a new problem.
body: During a Saturday rush, Lee, a new barista, mixed up two orders. Sam snapped at him in front of the queue. Lee mentions it to you quietly on Monday.
How do you raise it with Sam?

options.text: "Try to be a bit nicer to the team, okay?"
options.feedback: Quick and gentle, but vague. Sam can't tell what to change, and he may hear it as a judgment of his character.

options.text: "On Saturday when Lee mixed up the orders, you snapped at him at the counter. He went quiet for the rest of the shift. What was going on?"
options.feedback: This is **giving feedback**: soon, private, one specific behavior and its effect, then a question. Sam gets something he can act on and a chance to explain.

options.text: Save it for his review next month
options.feedback: You avoid an awkward talk today. But the moment fades, Lee keeps working with it, and Sam learns that snapping is acceptable.

cards.title: Feedback lands on the behavior, not the person.
body: Sam explains he was stressed about the queue. You agree on what he can do next time: step in, fix the order, and talk to Lee after the rush.

Then you add something easy to skip. You tell him the last ten closes were spotless, and the openers noticed. **Specific praise** tells a new lead which habits to keep, just as specific correction tells him what to change.

image.label: Owner and shift lead talking at a quiet table after closing
image.brief: 영업이 끝난 카페 구석 테이블. 사장과 교대 리더가 커피를 앞에 두고 편하게 대화. 배경에 깨끗하게 정리된 카운터. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Order matters, and so does restraint.
body: Feedback only works against an expectation that was already clear. If you correct people on standards you never stated, they'll feel ambushed, and they'll be right.
But don't turn every task into a checklist. Spell out the outcome and the few non-negotiables. Leave the *how* to your lead, or you'll end up with an order-taker instead of a lead.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse night shift.
body: You run a small distribution warehouse. You promoted Ana, your fastest picker, to night-shift lead. Since then, trucks keep leaving with wrong items, and customers are calling.

options.text: Tell Ana the errors have to stop
options.feedback: It names the outcome but not the standard or the check. Ana knows you're unhappy, not what "good" looks like or how she'll know she's there.

options.text: Agree with Ana on the outcome, a scan check before each pallet is sealed, and a short error count each morning
options.feedback: **Setting expectations** first gives you both a shared target. Then the morning count gives you specific moments for **feedback**, good and bad.

options.text: Move a day-shift checker onto nights to catch mistakes
options.feedback: Errors may drop this week, but Ana no longer owns the result. You've added cost and taught her that quality is someone else's job.

cards.softwareNote: The same move works when a developer becomes a team lead: agree what a good release looks like and how you'll measure it before you comment on the first one.

cards.title: Agree on done first. Then give feedback against it.
body: You used two ideas from this unit. **Setting expectations** turned a hidden target into an outcome, a standard, a deadline and a check. **Giving feedback** then worked because it was soon, specific and tied to a standard you both knew.
**Try it today:** pick one task someone on your team owns. Write one sentence on what done looks like. Ask them to write theirs, then compare.
